articles.title: Gaza: Indiscriminate Israeli gunfire kills and terrorises displaced families
articles.description:
Gaza: Indiscriminate Israeli gunfire kills and terrorises displaced families

    
    

          
      
      
        Submitted by 
Abdallah al-Naami
 on 
Mon, 11/02/2026 - 13:47

        
      
    
      
    
                From children playing out to families queuing for food, indiscriminate Israeli shooting has made daily life a struggle for survival across Gaza
                      
                  
                  

  


                  Safia Abo Amra hold a photo of her granddaughter Fatima al-Bayouk, who was killed by Israeli gunfire earlier this month (Abdallah al-Naami/MEE)
                  Off
                  After finishing her homework, Fatima al-Bayouk went to play with her cousins outside her grandmother’s home in Deir al-Balah, central Gaza, when an Israeli bullet struck her neck.

Moments later, the eight-year-old Palestinian girl returned home trembling, blood soaking her shirt. She screamed that her cousin had been shot, unaware that she had been hit herself.

The bullet had lodged in her lung. After a week in hospital, she died from her injuries.

For her grandmother, Safia Abo Amra, Bayouk - the sole survivor of her immediate family in an earlier Israeli air strike - was far more than a granddaughter. She had become her closest companion and the centre of her life.

“Fatima was my best friend. We did everything together, cooking, going on walks; we even slept on the same mattress. I have seven sons and six daughters, yet Fatima was more precious to me than all of them,” Abo Amra told Middle East Eye.
  
    



  



Despite everything she had endured, Bayouk had brought joy back into her grandmother’s life. Her uncle Ahmad Abo Amra remembered her as a bright, cheerful girl whose smile lifted the spirits of those around her.


'My life was attached to Fatima’s. I wish I could die after her'

- Safia Abo Amra, Palestinian grandmother 


“The best thing about Fatima was her smile that always brought joy to everyone around her. She was smart, responsible and loved happy occasions like weddings and family gatherings,” he said.

Her death reflects a wider pattern of indiscriminate Israeli gunfire that has become a daily threat to Palestinians across the Gaza Strip, particularly displaced families living near the so-called Yellow Line.

Israeli shooting from military positions, tanks and quadcopter drones has killed and wounded hundreds of civilians since the October 2025 ceasefire. It has also disrupted access to basic necessities and made everyday activities dangerous.

As Israel expands its control over more of the territory, families increasingly find themselves exposed to gunfire, with little protection and few places to seek safety.

A life cut short

For Bayouk’s family, her death was particularly devastating. She had already survived the loss of her immediate family in the early days of Israel’s genocide.

On 13 December 2023, an Israeli air strike targeted their home in Khan Younis, southern Gaza, killing her family. Bayouk survived and went to live with her grandmother in Deir al-Balah, where Abo Amra and other relatives tried to rebuild her life amid the devastation of the war.


'With her beautiful soul, she was the one to help me through my grief for my daughter and grandchildren'

- Safia  Abo Amro


“We did our best to provide everything Fatima needed and make her feel cared for and surrounded by people who love her,” Abo Amra said.

“I wanted to make up for the loss of her family, but with her beautiful soul, she was the one to help me through my grief for my daughter and grandchildren.”

Education remained an important part of Bayouk’s life as she grew up in her grandmother’s home. Concerned for her safety, Abo Amra refused to send her to a UN school after hearing that Israeli stray bullets frequently reached the area. Instead, she paid monthly fees to enrol her in a local school.

“I walked Fatima to school every day. She was very smart and always did her homework before playing,” Abo Amra said.

Her death reopened the grandmother’s wounds.

“I was shocked and couldn't speak or move. Her death was twice as painful for me; it reminded me of my daughter and grandchildren who were killed at the beginning of the war,” Abo Amra said. 

“My life was attached to Fatima’s. I wish I could die after her.”

  
  
      



    Fatima al-Bayouk liked to dress well, her family says (Abdallah al-Naami/MEE)
  









Despite her young age, Bayouk left a lasting impression on those around her. She loved dressing up, particularly for family celebrations.

Her uncle Reda Abo Amra remembered how much she enjoyed choosing new clothes. The family had recently bought her winter clothes, but she never got the chance to wear them.

“She always liked to be well-dressed. We bought her new clothes for winter, but she was killed before she could wear them,” he told MEE.
  
    



  



Bayouk was not the first member of her family to be killed by Israeli gunfire. Six months before her death, her uncle Masoud Abo Amra, who was born with a mental disability, was shot in the neck while visiting his sister in Khan Younis.

“Masoud was Fatima's favourite uncle. She was devastated when she bid him farewell,” Ahmad said.

‘When the shooting starts, life stops’

For displaced families in Gaza, Israeli gunfire is not only a deadly threat but also a constant disruption to daily life.

Zaid al-Kafarna, 19, and his family of 10 were displaced from northern Gaza to the Um Duhair area, south of Deir al-Balah, days before the October 2025 ceasefire came into effect.

Kafarna said Israeli shooting was initially “occasional” and took place some distance from their tents. But it gradually became more frequent and moved closer to the camp. Over the past three months, he said, it had become a daily threat, frequently causing deaths, injuries and damage. 


  

  Gaza family mourns boys killed by Israel along Yellow Line
    Read More »


“I miraculously survived stray bullets several times. My friend and neighbour, Mohammad Aqel, was killed a few weeks ago by a stray bullet while he was preparing to return to northern Gaza,” Kafarna told MEE.

His mother, Shereen al-Kafarna, was recently wounded by an Israeli bullet while inside their tent. She described how the shooting brings life in the camp to a standstill.

“When the shooting starts, life stops in our camp. Neighbours warn each other. We leave everything and hold the children, then lie on the ground to avoid the bullets hitting around us. Everyone is terrified, especially the children,” she said.

The gunfire also disrupts Palestinians' efforts to secure basic necessities, including food and water.

“Sometimes while we are waiting in queues for water and food, Israeli tanks and quadcopter drones start shooting directly towards us,” Zaid said.

“Everyone panics. We lie on the ground at the side of the road, watching the aid trucks carrying our food and water drive away to escape the bullets. On those days, we don't have anything to eat or drink.” 

Nowhere to go

The pattern of daily Israeli shootings near the Yellow Line, alongside the ongoing expansion of Israel’s buffer zone in Gaza, raised questions among families about whether the gunfire is as random as it appears.

Many believe that the shootings appear to form part of a military tactic to force Palestinian families out of their homes and tents, allowing Israel to expand its control over more territory through force.
  
    



  



In the year following the ceasefire, Israeli control over Gaza grew from 53 to 70 percent, reflecting what the Palestinians describe as a systematic policy of territorial expansion.

Families living near the Yellow Line said the threat of stray bullets had forced several others to leave their camps.

“Watching families leave our camp every day makes us feel even more afraid. We wish we could move away from the bullets, but we have nowhere to go,” Shereen told MEE. 

“Even if we had somewhere to go, we can't afford the extremely expensive cost of transportation.”

With few options for escape, some families have resorted to building small sand barriers and digging trench-like holes inside and between their tents to shelter from the bullets.

  
  
      



    Shadi Siam dug a trench for his family next to their tent to take cover from Israeli gunfire (Abdallah al-Naami/MEE)
  











Next to his tent, Shadi Siam dug a small trench to protect his family of five.

“I fear for my children's lives every time I hear Israeli stray bullets flying low,” Siam told MEE.

“My children wake up terrified, and I carry them to the hole where we all hide for two to five hours until the shooting stops,” he added.

“I don't know how I will protect them when the winter comes, and the hole becomes unusable.”

articles.title: ‘Death is closer than school’: Yemen’s children struggle with war trauma
articles.description:
‘Death is closer than school’: Yemen’s children struggle with war trauma

    
    

          
      
      
        Submitted by 
MEE correspondent
 on 
Mon, 11/02/2026 - 09:10

        
      
    
      
    
                Renewed fighting around Taiz has left children with nightmares, bedwetting and constant fear, while schools remain closed and psychological support is scarce
                      
                  
                  

  


                  A woman sits with two children in a classroom converted into a temporary shelter for displaced people at Sawkani school, north of Aden, Yemen, 15 September 2026 (AFP)
                  Off
                  In October, as clashes reached Taghreed Abdulellah’s area, located about 30km from Yemen's Taiz city, the mother of three found herself unable to flee with her children, as battles had already broken out in their village.

She had no choice but to gather her children, aged four, seven and 10, in the hallway to protect them from potential blasts or shrapnel coming through the windows.

“Their father wasn’t at home; it was just them and me. The clashes were outside, and an explosion went off right near our home, leaving the children terrified and crying for hours,” Abdulellah told Middle East Eye. 

“I couldn’t stop them from crying; in fact, I broke down and joined them at times.”

When the fighting quieted down, the children would stop crying, and some neighbours visited to boost their morale.
  
    



  



However, as soon as the battles flared up again, the crying resumed.

“This continued for four days until the fierce battles moved away from our area. But my children’s lives have completely changed for the worse,” she explained.

“My children are always angry, and the two younger ones are now suffering from bedwetting, while the eldest constantly talks about losing his life and believes he will be killed at any moment, rather than thinking about his studies and future as he used to.” 

Abdulellah’s children used to sleep in their own room, but since the fighting started, they do not dare to sleep alone. The whole family now sleeps in one room, with the two younger children sleeping in their mother’s arms.

“Nightmares terrify them every night, and during the day they refuse to leave the house because they feel they will be killed or injured if they go outside. So, they spend the entire day indoors,” Abdulellah said.

Battles in Taiz    

Public schools across Taiz governorate, including Taiz city and rural areas, have been closed since 4 October, as it is unsafe for children to attend school.

It is also unsafe for children to play outside, as shelling and air strikes hit almost every district in the area. 
  
    



  



Abdulellah believes it is unsafe for her children to go outside, yet she wants them to be able to so they can resume a normal life and heal from the psychological trauma they are facing.


  

  Yemen war: Taiz villagers face tough choices as fighters move in
    Read More »


“It is the first time in my life that I have seen my children feel so lost. They don’t want to play, they don’t want to study, and they only talk about the war. I am worried this will impact the rest of their lives even when normal life returns.”

On 4 October, Houthi forces advanced into large areas of Taiz governorate, taking control of most of the governorate and seizing all roads leading to Taiz city.

Battles are currently ongoing around Taiz city and in rural areas, as the Houthis, officially known as Ansar Allah, attempt to push from Taiz toward Lahij governorate while also trying to take full control of Taiz city.

Saudi-led air strikes have targeted Houthi forces in the rural areas of Taiz and around Taiz city, which have also taken a heavy toll on children in those areas.

The World Health Organization has reported that 1,677 people were killed and more than 7,395 injured across Yemen between August and late October 2026 amid renewed clashes between government forces and Houthis.

The executive manager of the Taiz Human Rights Centre civil society organization, Mazen Aqlan, told MEE that 19 children were killed and 49 injured in Taiz governorate in October 2026. 

Severe psychological impact   

Odai, 13, is a child in Taiz city whose life has also completely changed. He used to spend his mornings at school and his afternoons playing with friends. But since 4 October, he has spent most of his days and nights scrolling through his phone, only leaving the house briefly to sit with friends and adults under a nearby tree.

The main issue, however, lies in the photos and videos he views on his mobile, along with the stories he hears from adults about what happened in 2015 when fighting reached their neighbourhood and civilians, including children, were killed or injured. 

“Life isn’t easy, and death is close to everyone,” Odai told MEE. “We were focused on our studies and weren’t aware that a person could lose their life in a single minute. That is what happened to many people, both nowadays and during the last war.”


  

  'If Houthi shelling does not kill us, the diseases will': Yemenis in besieged Taiz bemoan neglect
    Read More »


Odai, who is in the seventh grade, appears mature for his age, but the ongoing developments and the stories he hears have shifted his priorities from his education to thoughts of the afterlife, something that is not typical for a child his age.

When asked about his priorities and whether they should focus on his studies, he laughed and said: “Studying is important, but there is no guarantee we will stay alive until schools reopen. Death is closer to us than resuming our education.”

MEE spoke with Odai’s father, in his 50s, who preferred to remain anonymous. He confirmed that Odai was not like this until last month, when he heard a story about a child killed in the city and saw related photos and videos, leaving him deeply affected.

“We do our best to keep our children away from the fighting. We keep them at home and don’t allow them to venture outside, especially to far areas, but it is difficult to keep a child mentally stable in this environment,” Odai’s father told MEE.

“Mobile phones and the stories they hear from friends leave a severe psychological impact on children, especially when they see photos of killed children. That is out of our control.”

He added that such horrifying scenes impact even adults like himself, not just children. He believes the best solution is for local authorities and organisations to provide immediate psychological support during these difficult times.

“During wartime, everyone worries about the physical safety of their children, and only a few care about their psychological well-being - which is just as important, as its long-term impact can be devastating,” he said.

Gap between needs and support

The Taiz Human Rights Centre's Aqlan told MEE: “There are more than 100,000 children in Taiz governorate who have witnessed the horrors of war and been traumatised by its shells, explosions and tragedies. They are in urgent need of psychological care.”

He identified the group most in need of psychological support as the families who have lost loved ones, had their homes shelled, been displaced or have directly suffered from the consequences of the war. 

  
  
      



    Women and children gather at a temporary shelter for displaced people at Shawkani school, north of Aden, Yemen, 15 September 2026 (AFP)
  




  
    



  









In mid-September, prior to the recent escalation around Taiz city, the UN children's agency Unicef reported that over 57,000 children had been displaced in just a two-week period.

While the Taiz Human Rights Centre estimates that over 100,000 children need psychological support in the governorate, the UN reported earlier this year, before the recent military escalation, that 12.2 million children across the country were in need of humanitarian assistance.

The Social Affairs and Labour Office in Taiz governorate stated on Sunday that non-governmental humanitarian organisations operating in the governorate provided psychosocial support services to 719 children, while 219 boys and girls received psychological first aid sessions.

Future at risk  

Psychologist Saba al-Sabri, who works with several institutions providing psychological support in Taiz, confirmed that clear behavioural changes in children have been observed over the past month.

“These behaviours include non-acceptance of others, grief over loss, continuous fear, nervousness, bedwetting, clinging to parents even during sleep, and a total loss of motivation to learn because they believe they will die or become disabled, all of which severely affect the children’s future,” Sabri told MEE. 


  

  Yemen: Parents in Taiz demand answers over alleged rape of their children
    Read More »


She said that the counselling sessions provided by humanitarian initiatives and organisations remain far too few compared to the immense need that has persisted for over 11 years.

“These recent events have added new children to the list of those in need, making psychological support vital to preserving the next generation.”

Sabri pointed out that some parents do not realise the severity of psychological trauma on children, and instead focus solely on basic survival, which represents a disaster for the child.

“Ignoring a child’s feelings and failing to sit and communicate with them leaves a deep negative impact on their well-being.”

Most children currently do not leave their homes. Sabri noted that children are naturally energetic and need to play outside; depriving them of this heightens stress and nervousness, weakens their personality development and worsens their mood.

Abdulellah, the mother of the three children who witnessed the fighting and were traumatised, strongly believes in psychological treatment, but it remains inaccessible to them.

“If psychological treatment were available, I wouldn’t hesitate to take my children. But we are in a time of war, and it is hard to access such services since they are usually only available in the city.”

                After finishing her homework, Fatima al-Bayouk went to play with her cousins outside her grandmother’s home in Deir al-Balah, central Gaza, when an Israeli bullet struck her neck.

Moments later, the eight-year-old Palestinian girl returned home trembling, blood soaking her shirt. She screamed that her cousin had been shot, unaware that she had been hit herself.

The bullet had lodged in her lung. After a week in hospital, she died from her injuries.

                  Israeli forces have killed 19 Palestinians in the Gaza Strip since Saturday, according to the Palestinian Health Ministry.

The ministry said on Tuesday afternoon that six people had been killed in the previous 24 hours, following 13 deaths over the weekend.

One Palestinian succumbed to his wounds on Tuesday morning after Israeli forces bombed the displacement camp where he was staying in Khan Younis.

Another was killed in an air strike targeting a group of people at the University College of Applied Sciences (UCAS) in Khan Younis.

Israeli attacks on school pupils and university students across the Gaza Strip have increased in recent weeks, following the start of the new academic year.
  
    



  



At least 14 pupils and four teachers were killed in Gaza in October, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Education and Higher Education.

Three employees of the Islamic University were also killed in an Israeli bombing on campus last month.

The ministry further reported that more than 97 percent of schools and universities in the Gaza Strip have been destroyed by Israeli attacks.

The remaining educational institutions and alternative learning facilities continue to face the threat of further attacks and damage, it added. 

Elsewhere, Gaza's Ministry of Interior reported an Israeli air strike targeting police officers and security personnel in the Al-Mawasi area of Khan Younis.

Several people were killed and wounded, the ministry said, without providing a final death toll. 

Violations of ceasefire

The attacks come as Israel continues to violate the October 2025 ceasefire in Gaza.
  
    



  



The US-mediated agreement was intended to halt Israel's genocide by ending the bombardment and lifting restrictions on the entry of humanitarian aid.

However, Israel has continued to carry out near-daily air strikes and demolitions of homes.

According to the Palestinian Health Ministry, Israeli forces have killed nearly 1,600 Palestinians since the ceasefire came into effect, including more than 340 children.

A further 5,700 people have been wounded.

The overall Palestinian death toll since the genocide began in October 2023 has reached at least 74,600, according to the ministry. Thousands more people remain missing or buried under the rubble.

Israeli authorities have also continued to impose tight restrictions on the entry of aid and goods into Gaza.

An average of just 200 trucks have been allowed into the territory each day, well below the agreed 600 and the estimated minimum required to meet Gaza's needs.

According to Gaza's Government Media Office, Israeli forces have committed 5,989 violations of the ceasefire since it took effect on 11 October 2025.

These include air strikes, shootings, home demolitions, raids and arbitrary arrests.

articles.title: US elections 2026: Can a Democrat-controlled Senate thwart Trump's agenda?
articles.description:
US elections 2026: Can a Democrat-controlled Senate thwart Trump's agenda?

    
    

          
      
      
        Submitted by 
Yasmine El-Sabawi
 on 
Mon, 11/02/2026 - 16:31

        
      
    
      
    
                In short: Maybe, and much of it will centre on how debates are framed moving forward
                      
                  
                  

  


                  Voters cast their ballots at a polling station inside a shopping mall in Anchorage, Alaska, on 2 November 2026, a day ahead of the US midterm elections (Charly Triballeau/AFP)
                  Off
                  American voters are fed up, as almost every conversation with them will demonstrate, regardless of party affiliation. 

In the lead-up to the 3 November midterm elections, early voting has seen an unprecedented turnout of 56 million Americans, a stunning figure considering non-presidential election years have traditionally had low turnout rates. 

President Donald Trump's approval rating is lower than that of his last three predecessors when their first midterm election season rolled around, including his own first term in office. 

If both the polling and the predictions of Republican analysts are anything to go by, Democrats will not only retake the House after Tuesday's midterm elections, but also take the powerful Senate, and boast the most governors across the 50 states. 

But there may be little change in actual legislation, and a lot more change in narrative and framing in the US legislature. 
  
    



  



Rina Shah, a former Republican congressional adviser, told Middle East Eye that in the Senate, the workable strategy will be refusal - not reversal - of administration policy.

For example, as Trump and his party try to appoint conservative judges to federal courts, liberal senators could block them. Federal judges have been crucial to the release of several critics of Israel from immigration detention, after Secretary of State Marco Rubio cancelled their visas and US Green Cards. 

"The Senate majority controls the calendar, committee gavels, and confirmations. That means it can slow-walk or block ambassadors and national security nominees, hold oversight hearings with subpoena power, and use appropriations and the National Defense Authorisation Act to put conditions on things like arms sales, troop deployments, and war powers," she said. 

But Trump will almost certainly veto any bills that he doesn't agree with.

"That's partly the point," Shah said. "Even a vetoed bill forces Republicans to go on the record and frames the 2028 debate. The real teeth are in must-pass bills like government funding and defence authorisation, which he can't easily veto without owning a [government] shutdown or a lapse in defence funding."

What power looks like

But Trump hasn't been afraid to allow for the government to shut down, as he dukes it out with Democratic lawmakers. He has done it twice. 

To make a real dent in the Senate that can overcome a presidential veto, as well as account for a couple of defections from their party on certain issues - and even convict a US president or members of his cabinet in an impeachment trial - Democrats will need to secure at least 60 seats, which is not going to happen this cycle.
  
    



  



That means there will still need to be some heavy negotiating - and compromising - to try to bring the opposition on side. 


  

  US elections: Races to watch in the 2026 midterms
    Read More »


"It's going to be a matter of how they frame issues and what questions they put to the [Senate], as to whether or not they can convince Republicans to come on board with any particular measure," Jennifer Hendrixson White, a former House Foreign Affairs Committee staffer, told MEE.

She is now a visiting scholar in the American Statecraft programme at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.

"Whereas Republicans may have been less likely to challenge the president in the early part of his term, perhaps there will be a little more willingness to do so" now, given their terms will outlast Trump's remaining time in office, Hendrixson White explained.

"Additionally, if Congress really focuses on addressing and reclaiming some of their traditional Article One responsibilities, and they frame the questions before the Senate in those types of terms, they may be able to convince Republicans to support those measures."

Article One of the US Constitution lays out the design and responsibilities of US lawmakers as a check and balance on the powers of the president.

In the Senate, Democrats will need to hold onto all 47 of their current seats and also flip four Republican seats to win. Texas, Maine, North Carolina, and Alaska are likely to fill those slots, with Iowa and Ohio also hotly contested.

There is near-universal agreement that Democrats will gain control of the lower chamber of Congress, which is the House of Representatives. 

The upper chamber, however, is where the heavyweights sit, because senators have six-year terms that untether them from the four-year presidency or a two-year House term. 

YouGov's survey on the Senate races on Monday shows many are neck and neck, but that Democrats have the advantage. 

On Polymarket, nearly 75 percent of those putting money on control of the Senate predict a Democratic sweep of both chambers. 

On ABC News on Sunday, former New Jersey Governor Chris Christie and former House Speaker Kevin McCarthy - both Republicans - said they expect the same. Christie also predicted a final outcome of 27 Democratic governors out of 36 states that have gubernatorial elections.

There has been consensus from voters across the political spectrum that prices are too high, and that the Trump administration's agenda is overly aggressive, owing to violent encounters with immigration agents on the streets, and a joint war with Israel on Iran that has, by all accounts, continued into its ninth month with no end in sight. 
  
    



  



Trump very specifically pledged affordability, safety, and an end to all wars in his 2024 campaign. 

The Israel problem

On some questions that have become important to voters across the political spectrum - like the necessity of an unconditional US-Israel relationship - change will take time, but it will begin with open discussion on the Senate floor. 


'There will be a push to conditionalise military aid to Israel'

- David McCuan, professor at Sonoma State University


"There will be a push to conditionalise military aid to Israel. That's much more of a 'hot potato'" than trying to sanction the war on Iran, for example, David McCuan, a political science professor at Sonoma State University, told MEE. 

"But if you see some elements of the Democratic left feeling emboldened, whether that's [Abdul] El-Sayed winning in Michigan, coupled with Bernie [Sanders], all of a sudden you have a few votes where you can get over a hurdle to at least have the debate."

Israel's current unfavourability in the US, particularly among liberal youth, "cannot be ignored or punted", Wajahat Ali, a Daily Beast columnist and author of the book Go Back to Where You Came From, told MEE. 

"This will be a litmus test issue. I've been saying it for two years. Any Democrat that thinks they have national aspirations and they could still be a pro-Israel hawk is sorely mistaken," he said. 

"Democratic leaders and donors have to make a decision. Do we go scorched earth and burn everything down for Israel, or do we evolve and reform and meet the moment and the people?"

Revenge or move forward?

Since the Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, and the subsequent Israeli assault on Gaza that the United Nations and Holocaust scholars have called a genocide, positive views of Israel have sunk to an all-time low in the US.

"This administration has been relatively less susceptible to political pressure than previous administrations might have been demonstrated to be," Hendrixson White told MEE.

"I would like to believe that Congress will absolutely be clever and creative in the way that they're framing debates, and that they're able to generate a degree of consensus on the most important matters," she said.

"Where I think there's a risk is if Congress does what's easy: The non-binding political statements. You end up spending a lot of legislative time on issues that ultimately don't force the president's hand... How much time is going to be put into anti-corruption and investigation-type efforts?"

That's where Democrats will also be under tremendous pressure.


  

  'Despicable betrayal': Haley Stevens endorses Republican candidate over party nominee Abdul El-Sayed
    Read More »


Critics of the president have been demanding investigations into his financial dealings at home and abroad, such as his acceptance of a plane as a gift from Qatar; his connection to the convicted child sex trafficker Jeffrey Epstein; and how Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner's voluntary role as a peace negotiator for the administration has benefited him personally.

Trump, his family, and his cabinet deny any wrongdoing.

McCuan, who frequently explains US election outcomes and implications to foreign diplomats, said a Democrat-controlled Senate will likely be forward-facing rather than focused on accountability for the past.

"There's two ways of thinking about midterms. You can think about midterms as referendums or as backlash. Most of the data in political science, most of the quality studies, are that midterms are a backlash," he said.

This "means Democrats need a counter-programme on Capitol Hill, principally within the Senate, that advances an agenda that's important for 2028".

Given how the US political calendar works, candidates who want to run for president have to start their exploratory committees now so they can gauge support levels, fundraise, and hire staff.

"The 2028 election starts on November 4th, and so that means you have to meet voters on issues of affordability, on gas prices, on diesel, on what's happening with groceries," McCuan told MEE. "It's less about investigations and impeachment. Not an absence of those things, but much less about those things, and much more about an agenda that meets voters where they're at and concerns over their pocketbooks."

Ali called such a move "a major fear".

"I do not have faith in the current leadership of the Democratic Party," he told MEE.

"I'm not talking about all Democrats, and I say that based on their own actions and rhetoric. I do not believe that [top Senate Democrat Chuck] Schumer and [top House Democrat Hakeem] Jeffries are made for this moment or built for this fight. They spend their time attacking Medicare-For-All, attacking Democratic Socialists, taking money from Aipac, punching to the left, having secret meetings with Jared Kushner," he said.

"If they do win on Tuesday night, they are sorely mistaken if they believe this is a realignment of America towards Democrats. Oh no. This is a realignment from MAGA, and a rental. This is a very brief rental."

The 120th Congress will be sworn in on 3 January 2027.
